1.explanation:
All of these functions live in the heart of the ESLint code-path analysis engine and control how logical operators and nullish coalescing are turned into forks and merges in the control-flow graph:

• isHandledLogicalOperator: decides which operators ("&&", "||", "??") get special short-circuit handling. If it’s wrong here, `??` combined with `&&` won’t fork correctly.

• preprocess: this helper is responsible for creating a new fork when entering the right side of a logical expression. It must recognize that when the left side of `&&` is falsy, control should still move to `c` under `??`.

• processCodePathToEnter / processCodePathToExit: these methods in CodePathAnalyzer drive the actual creation and closing of code-path segments when nodes are entered or exited. They use the information from isHandledLogicalOperator and preprocess to build the graph. Any mistake here will mis-emit the onCodePathStart/onCodePathSegmentStart events for the missing branch.

Fixing and/or augmenting these functions so that `(a && b) ?? c` produces three distinct segments (truthy `a`→`b`, falsy `a`→`c`, and falsy `b`→`c`) will resolve the missing arrow in the graph.

2.explanation:
All of the flagged methods live in `code-path-analyzer.js` and contribute to how logical operators (including `??`) are recognized and how the code-path is forked.  

• isHandledLogicalOperator(operator): Currently treats `??` exactly like `&&`/`||`.  It needs to distinguish nullish coalescing so that only nullish values (not all falsy values) cause evaluation of the right side.  

• isForkingByTrueOrFalse(node): Decides whether a logical test forks into two separate flow segments.  The predicate here must be updated so that a `??` expression only forks on nullish, not on every false or zero.  

• preprocess(analyzer, node): Handles the creation of new fork contexts when entering child nodes—specifically it currently forks unconditionally at the “right” of any handled logical operator.  It should only fork for `??` when the left side can be nullish.  

• processCodePathToExit(analyzer, node): Mirrors the logic of `preprocess` when exiting nodes.  It currently closes the left‐false branch for all handled operators, which causes the missing path into `c`.  It must be altered to preserve the branch into the right side of `??` when the left side is non-nullish but falsy.  

By updating these methods to respect the nullish-only short-circuit semantics of `??`, the analyzer will produce the correct three paths for `(a && b) ?? c`.
2.bug_scenario: The user is calling ESLint’s code-path analysis on the expression `(a && b) ?? c`.  The generated control-flow graph treats the nullish operator `??` the same as `||` or `&&`, so it creates exactly the same two branches it would for `(a || b) ?? c`—either (a→b→…) or (a→exit)—and never presents the third “a false but not null” path into `c`.  In reality, `(a && b) ?? c` should short-circuit into `c` only if `a && b` is nullish (e.g. `null` or `undefined`), but the analyzer treats any falsy `a` (including `false` or `0`) as if it bypasses `c` entirely.  The image shows the DOT graph with only two branches instead of three, so the analyzer is missing the “a false but not null” path that leads into `c`.
